How to Read a Creator Media Kit

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 7 August 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

A creator media kit is a sales document prepared by the seller. Read past the follower count to median engagement, real demographics and repeat sponsors, ask for the numbers it leaves out, and test on cost-per-outcome terms before buying a package. Buyers have reason to be careful: a third of US creator ad buyers told the IAB in 2025 that finding the right creators was their biggest hurdle, and the US Federal Trade Commission now bans buying or selling fake follower and view counts used to misrepresent influence.

A media kit is the document a creator or publisher sends to a company considering paying them: audience size, demographics, engagement, past partners, formats offered, and rates. It is a sales document, prepared by the seller, and it should be read as one.

The money involved is no longer small. The IAB estimated US advertisers spent $37 billion with creators in 2025, and Goldman Sachs Research estimated in 2023 that brand deals make up about 70% of creator income. When most of a creator's revenue comes from sponsors, the media kit is the creator's most important sales tool, and it is written accordingly.

What is usually in it

SectionWhat it showsWhat it hidesWhat to ask for instead
Audience sizeFollowers, subscribers, listeners, recipients by platformInactive accounts, bots, followers from years agoViews or reach per post over ninety days
EngagementAverage likes, comments, shares, views, opens, clicksSelection of best posts; bought engagementMedian over the last thirty posts
DemographicsAge, gender, location, sometimes interestsWhether the audience buys your categoryShare of audience in your markets and roles
Past partnersLogos of companies that paid beforeWho paid twiceRepeat sponsors and a reference
Formats and ratesPrices per post, mention, story, integration, placementFlexibility, performance termsA first piece on cost-per-outcome terms
Case studiesOne past campaign with resultsHow the result was measuredThe tracking method and the sponsor's own view

What each number means, and what it hides

Follower count is the least informative figure and the one most prominently displayed. It includes inactive accounts, bots, and people who followed years ago for a different reason. On platforms where reach is algorithmic, followers barely predict how many people see a post. Rival IQ's 2025 benchmark of brand accounts, vendor data that divides interactions by follower count, found median engagement fell 16% on Instagram, 34% on TikTok and 48% on X year on year. A follower count says less each year about who interacts with a post.

Average engagement is more useful, and is routinely calculated on the creator's best-performing recent posts. Ask for the median over the last thirty posts, not the average over the best ten. One viral post can double an average; it barely moves a median. Expect smaller accounts to post higher rates. HypeAuditor's 2025 report, vendor analysis of 76 million Instagram accounts, put nano-influencers (1,000 to 10,000 followers) at a 2.19% engagement rate, the highest of any tier. A large account with a rate well above its tier deserves a second look.

Bought numbers are now a legal question as well as a commercial one. The FTC's August 2024 rule on reviews and testimonials prohibits buying or selling bot-generated or hijacked-account metrics, "fake indicators of social media influence", where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them for a commercial purpose. Ask the creator to confirm in writing that no followers, views or engagement were bought.

Demographics come from platform analytics and are reasonably reliable for age, gender, and country. They say nothing about whether the audience buys the category. A finance creator's audience may be mostly other finance creators.

Past partners tell you who paid once. They do not tell you who paid twice, which is the figure that matters.

Rates are a starting position. They vary by month, by how full the creator's calendar is, and by whether the deal is flat or performance-based.

A creator who returns to the follower count has told you what the media kit was for.

The numbers that are not on it

Audience overlap with other creators the company is considering. Share of audience in the geographies the product serves. Evidence that the audience has adopted products the creator recommended before. Retention: how many people who came through this creator last time are still customers. Whether the creator will accept cost-per-outcome terms, which reveals more about their confidence in their audience than any slide.

And the creator's other commercial relationships, including competitors and, in crypto, tokens they hold. The cost of missing this is documented. In October 2022 the US Securities and Exchange Commission settled with a celebrity who had been paid $250,000 to post about a crypto token without disclosing the payment; the settlement totalled $1.26 million. The SEC chair's statement was direct: promoters must disclose "when and how much they are paid to promote investing in securities." A brand that pays a creator who is also paid by, or invested in, a competing token inherits a disclosure problem.

The questions to ask

  1. May we see platform analytics directly, screen-shared, for the last ninety days?
  2. What did the last three sponsors in our category see, and may we speak to one?
  3. What share of your audience is in our markets?
  4. Would you do a first piece on a cost-per-outcome basis, with a tracked link, before we discuss a package?
  5. What are your current paid relationships, and are any in our category? Do you hold tokens or equity in anything you cover?
  6. What disclosure language do you use, and where does it appear?

The last question has a right answer. FTC guidance asks for disclosures that are hard to miss, placed with the endorsement, and, in video, given both in audio and in on-screen text. A creator who discloses only in a profile bio or behind a "more" link is a compliance risk for the brand as well as the creator.

A creator who answers those readily is a professional with a real audience. A creator who returns to the follower count has told you what the media kit was for.

Read it against the job

The kit describes the creator. The decision depends on the job: awareness, explanation, conversion, or authority in a specialist audience. A large, lightly engaged audience may suit the first and fail at the rest. A small, deeply trusting audience may do the opposite. Our guide to influencers, creators, KOLs and ambassadors sets out which kind of person sells which job.

JobWhat the kit must showTest before a package
AwarenessVerified reach in your marketsBranded search and direct traffic against a baseline
ExplanationWatch time or read depth on similar topicsQuestions and replies from the right roles
ConversionPast tracked sales in the categoryOne piece on a tracked link, paid per outcome
Specialist authorityAudience of practitioners, repeat sponsorsA reference call with a peer sponsor

Match the kit's numbers to the job, test small before committing, and pay for the outcome the job requires. Our playbook on campaign testing that reaches a decision covers how to size the test so the answer is usable.

lowob takeaways

  • Read it as a sales document. The seller chose which numbers to show.
  • Ask for medians and the missing numbers. Thirty-post median, audience in your markets, repeat sponsors, other paid relationships.
  • Get the no-fake-metrics promise in writing. Bought followers and views are a US federal rule issue.
  • Pay for the job. Test one piece on outcome terms before buying a package.

Common questions

How do I evaluate an influencer's media kit?

Treat it as a sales document. Look past follower count to median engagement, platform-sourced demographics and repeat sponsors, and ask to see platform analytics directly for the last ninety days.

What questions should I ask a creator before sponsoring them?

Ask to see analytics screen-shared, what the last three sponsors in your category saw, what share of the audience is in your markets, whether they will do a first piece on cost-per-outcome terms, and what paid relationships or holdings they have.

How can you tell if an influencer has fake followers?

Compare engagement to the norm for the account's size, look at the median rather than the average, and ask for screen-shared analytics. In the US, buying fake influence metrics for commercial use breaches an FTC rule, so ask for a written confirmation.

What is missing from most media kits?

Audience overlap with other creators, share of audience in your geographies, evidence of past product adoption, retention of customers they sent, and their other commercial relationships, including token holdings in crypto.
